The prosecution case is as follows :
2. PW22 is the first informant and Ex.P17 is his report to the police alleging accused 1 to 3 being responsible for the suicide committed by his sister, Kalavathi.

He alleged in his report that before the marriage of his sister Kalavathi was solemnized with accused No.1 on 04.11.2007 at Maluru, on the demand made by all the accused, his family had to pay cash of Rs.1,60,000/-, a gold chain, a ring and watch to the first accused.

The couple lived together cordially for about fifteen days after the marriage and thereafter the accused insisted his wife to bring a sum of Rs.1,00,000/- from her parental house as accused No.1 wanted capital for his NC: 2024:KHC:10146-DB television shop.
In this connection the deceased used to be harassed and ill-treated as PW22 or his father could not arrange for money.
The deceased was driven out of the house of the accused thereafter.

It was also alleged that the accused sold away the jewelleries worth Rs.3,00,000/-

sentences.text: PW22 prevailed upon his sister to settle the relationship between her and her husband by speaking to the elders of his community.
At that time the deceased made it clear that she was ready to live with her husband provided a separate residence was set up for them.
He stated in Ex.P22 that accused No.1 held out a threat to his wife that he would kill her brother, PW22 first and then kill the others in her family.
After all this, one day i.e., before the death, the deceased went to the village Koduru.
There she told her parents that she would bring grass for the cattle from the fields and left home, but did not come back.
On the morning of 07.06.2008 around 6.00 am one Laxman asked PW22 to come near the pump house situate in his land.
And going there he saw the dead body of his NC: 2024:KHC:10146-DB sister.

Suspecting that his sister committed suicide being unable to bear the torture and ill-treatment meted out to her by the accused, he approached the police with a report based on which the police registered an FIR in Crime No. 172/2008 for the offences punishable under Sections 498A and 304B of IPC, and Sections 3 and 4 of Dowry Prohibition Act read with Section 34 of IPC.
The investigation resulted in charge sheet being filed.
The trial court charged the accused for the offences under Sections 498A, 304B and 306 of IPC, and Sections 3, 4 and Section 6 of the Dowry Prohibition Act read with Section 34 of IPC.
The trial resulted in acquittal of the accused and hence these two appeals.

3. We have heard the argument of Sri A.P.Pulakeshi, learned counsel for the appellant in Crl.A.
2091/2017, Smt. K.P.Yashodha, learned HCGP for the State and Sri V.G.Tigadi, learned counsel for respondents 1 and 3 and Sri Rasheed Khan for respondent No.4 in both the appeals.
NC: 2024:KHC:10146-DB 4.
Smt. K.P.Yashodha argued that the findings recorded by the trial court for acquitting the accused are contrary to the evidence placed by the prosecution.

There is clear evidence that before the marriage was held, the accused demanded for dowry for Rs.2,00,000/- and some gold items and at last the brother and the father of the deceased had to agree for paying a sum of Rs.1,60,000/- and gold items to the accused.
The main witnesses may be closely related to the deceased, as it is usual in a case of this type and for that reason alone it is not justifiable to reject their testimonies.
It may be a fact that there may be some minor contradictions in their testimonies, but they do not dislodge the entire prosecution case.
This should have been the approach of the trial court.
She submitted that the main witnesses PWs12, 13, 14, 15, 19, 21 and 22 have clearly stated that there was demand for dowry prior to marriage and after the marriage.

The very fact that the deceased could not live in her matrimonial home for a longer period itself shows that she was subjected to ill-treatment as the demand of the accused NC: 2024:KHC:10146-DB for dowry was not satisfied.

The deceased committed suicide being unable to bear torture and her death being unnatural having taken place within seven years of marriage, the accused should have been held guilty of the offences punishable under Sections 498A, 304B of IPC and Sections 3, 4 and 6 of the Dowry Prohibition Act.
She referred to Exs.P18 and P21, the two note books containing the handwriting of the deceased and argued that they reveal the plight of the deceased which drove her to commit suicide.
The expert's opinion establishes that the handwritings in Exs. P18 and P21 are same and they were that of the deceased.
The trial court has failed to consider this evidence in proper perspective.

Though some of the witnesses have not supported, the testimonies of other witnesses who have not been discredited K N Perumal vs M S Krishna on 12 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16436410/
5 in the cross-examination clearly indicate that the accused were responsible for the unnatural death of the deceased.

sentences.text: She also argued that the trial court should have drawn presumptions according to section 113-B of the Indian Evidence Act.

. Sri. Pulakeshi, learned counsel for the appellant in Crl.A.No.2091/2017 reiterating the points urged by Smt. K.P.Yashodha, argued that though a few witnesses have turned hostile, the testimonies of PW12, PW13, PW19, PW21 and PW22 do clearly establish the prosecution case.
The trial court has not read the evidence properly.
The evidence is so clear that before the marriage, the accused actually demanded for Rs.2,00,000/-, but ultimately, they agreed for Rs.1,60,000/-.
They also demanded for gold jewelleries.
They were all given to accused No.1 fifteen days before the marriage.
The marriage did not last long due to further demand for Rs.1,00,000/- after the marriage.
The witnesses have spoken that Kalavathi herself revealed before them the way she used to be ill treated.
Their evidence is fortified by Ex.P18 in which there is a clear revealation of harassment on the deceased.

Referring to judgment of the Supreme Court in State of A.P. Vs. Raj Gopal Asawa and Another [(2004) 4 SCC 470], he argued that the demand for dowry itself would constitute an offence, and an - 11 - NC: 2024:KHC:10146-DB agreement in that regard is not necessary.

His argument is that improper appreciation of evidence is the result of acquittal judgment and for this reason, appeal deserves to be allowed.
6.

Keeping in mind the points of argument and the established principle that there cannot be interference with the acquittal judgment unless there is gross error and perversity in appreciation of evidence, if the evidence is put to scrutiny, the following is the picture obtainable.
7. There is no dispute that death of Kalavathi was unnatural within seven years of marriage which had taken place on 4.11.2007.
She committed suicide by consuming a poisonous substance.
The evidence of PW31, the doctor who conducted post mortem examination confirms it.
8. Now in regard to the demand for dowry said to have made before the marriage, the independent witnesses PW1 to PW7, PW9 and PW14 do not support.

PW12 is the sister, PW13 is the mother,
PW14 and PW19 are the relatives, PW21 is the father, and PW22 is the - 12 - NC: 2024:KHC:10146-DB brother of the deceased.
Of course they speak that there was a demand for dowry before the marriage, and they had to agree for cash of Rs.1,60,000/- and gold items as insisted by accused 1 to 4.

It appears that PW12 and PW22 have played a prominent role in the K N Perumal vs M S Krishna on 12 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16436410/
6 arrangement and performance of marriage.

sentences.text: PW12 was working in a private firm at Maluru, and in regard to mobilizing the money required for marriage, her evidence is that she borrowed a sum of Rs.1,50,000/- from Manjunath, PW4, but he has not testified the same.

To prove that they bought gold items, prosecution examined PW24, whose clear evidence is that though PW12 and PW22 were his customers, they did not purchase from him any gold item in connection with the marriage.
His evidence is that he made estimate of some ornaments prepared by somebody else.
His testimony is of no avail to prosecution for this reason.

PW15 to PW17 do not appear to be having a direct knowledge of marriage talks, all that can be inferred from their evidence is that they just came to know about marriage talks for which reason their evidence is of no - 13 - NC: 2024:KHC:10146-DB use.
Whatever may be the stance of the witnesses, there cannot be denial of marriage talks, but the evidence does not disclose semblance of truth in the actual negotiations.

Customarily, jewelleries appear to have been given to the bride and the groom, but giving of cash of Rs.1,60,000/- before the marriage, in spite of evidence by the related witnesses, has to be looked with askance.
9. In regard to post marriage demand for dowry, except the evidence of blood relatives and other relatives of the deceased, there is no buttressal from independent witnesses.

It is true, and arguable that this kind of a situation can only be established by the relatives of the deceased, and the legal position is also that a demand for dowry itself constitutes an offence as has been held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Raj Gopal Asawa (supra).

Still, the testimonies of the prominent witnesses is difficult to be acted upon because the real reason for suicide does not appear to be harassment on the deceased in connection with demand for dowry post marriage.

What - 14 - NC: 2024:KHC:10146-DB the evidence shows, assuming that the oral evidence of prominent witnesses is believable, is that accused No.1 sold away the jewelleries given at the time of marriage for his business purpose, and he was short of Rs.1,00,000/-, which he wanted to be made good by the father or brother or sister of the wife.
Expectation for financial help may not take the meaning of dowry.
10. The prosecution has come up with another reason for the death.
The allegation is that accused No.1 had illicit relationship with accused No.5, a married woman.
The witnesses consistently speak about it.
PW14 has stated that the deceased had once told him about relationship between accused No.1 and accused No.5.
PW27 is examined to prove a quarrel between the deceased and accused No.5.
It appears that the deceased had a suspicion that there might have existed illicit contact between her husband and accused No.5.
That apart the prosecution has introduced Ex.P.18, some writings of the deceased in a note book.

PW35 has given evidence by - 15 - K N Perumal vs M S Krishna on 12 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16436410/
7 NC: 2024:KHC:10146-DB

sentences.text: comparing the admitted handwriting of the deceased found in Ex.P21 that the hand writings in both the note books are of the same person.

If Ex.P18 is seen, it only shows the anguish of the deceased towards her husband not in connection with demand for money; it may be for other reason, probably the suspected intimacy between accused No.1 and accused No.5.
It is quite natural that a woman does not tolerate the extramarital relationship of her husband, and the reaction of a woman to this kind of a situation varies from person to person.
11. While cross-examining PW12 and PW22, they were suggested that accused No.1 had taken his wife to many doctors and hospitals to provide treatment to her.
Mere suggestions may not have evidentiary value, but the way the suggestions are given and the way the witnesses respond to the suggestions have a bearing on the assessment of evidence.
Here if PW22 denied all the suggestions in regard to treatment provided to the deceased by accused No.1, PW12 gave evasive answers to - 16 - NC: 2024:KHC:10146-DB the same type of suggestions.

If there was no truth in the suggestions,
PW12 should have denied them outrightly, but she neither admitted nor denied them; her answer was she did not know - which is nothing but an evasive answer.
The inference to be drawn is that probably the deceased did have certain health issues affecting her psychologically.
This inference can be drawn with the help of evidence given by DW2, a reputed psychiatrist.

12. DW1 and DW3 are two other doctors who might have treated the deceased for her some physiological conditions, but the evidence of DW2, which has a greater bearing shows that when he examined the deceased he noticed in her certain issues such as easily getting into arrogance, suicidal tendency, non co-operation with family members and anxiety.
He gave treatment to her.

To some extent, DW1 - another doctor has also stated that the deceased was suffering from hypothyroidism for seven years past and that a person suffering from hypothyroidism may develop other health disorders - 17 - NC: 2024:KHC:10146-DB including psychiatric manifestations.
Thus seen, the suggestions given to PW12 and PW22 cannot be outrightly rejected.
13. There is yet another reason owing to which prosecution case can be doubted.
PW36, PW37 and PW38 are the police officers.
Kalavathi was last seen alive on 06.06.2008.
Her dead body was found in the morning of 07.06.2008.
PW22 lodged FIR on 07.06.2008 with PW36.
On 09.06.2008, PW37 was directed by the Superintendent of Police to investigate into the matter.
PW37 began investigation on 12.06.2008.
On 04.07.2008 she handed over investigation to PW38.
In between 12.06.2008 till 04.07.2008, she did not record statements of the main witnesses.
PW38 has stated that he took over investigation on 04.08.2008.
And on 14.08.2008, he recorded the statements of the main witnesses.

There is no explanation as to why PW37 did not think it expedient to obtain the statements of the witnesses in between 12.06.2008 and 04.07.2008, even though those witnesses K N Perumal vs M S Krishna on 12 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16436410/
8 - 18 - NC: 2024:KHC:10146-DB were available.

entities.text: K N Perumal vs M S Krishna
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: PW38 also did not record the statements of the main witnesses immediately after taking over investigation.
Another important aspect is PW22 being the first informant did not enter the witness box as a first witness.
He waited till others adduced evidence.
The father, the mother and the sister of the deceased also entered the witness box late.
If they did so deliberately to watch how the other witnesses would fare in the court, their conduct must be viewed dubiously.
These two factors militate against the evidentiary value in testimonies of the main witnesses.
14. The net effect of evidence is, it is difficult to accept the prosecution version that harassment in relation to demand for dowry after the marriage led Kalavathi commit suicide.
15. The trial court may not have dealt with intricacies of evidence; it appears that it has appreciated the evidence from a different angle which is also possible.
Now, if it is possible to hold that the evidence given by the - 19 - NC: 2024:KHC:10146-DB main witnesses is believable, it is another view that can be taken.
The settled position is that if two views - one in favour of the accused are possible to be taken, its benefit must be given to accused.
16. The foregoing discussion takes us to conclude that the appeals are to be dismissed.
Ordered accordingly.

14. The net effect of evidence is, it is difficult to accept the prosecution version that harassment in relation to demand for dowry after the marriage led Kalavathi commit suicide.
The settled position is that if two views - one in favour of the accused are possible to be taken, its benefit must be given to accused.

Ordered accordingly.
